title: Supreme Court Flags Three-Month Delay in TMC Rebel MPs' Disqualification Case
excerpt: A bench headed by Chief Justice Surya Kant called the lapse of three months a red flag, kept Abhishek Banerjee's petition alive to monitor the Speaker's proceedings, and recorded that the 20 MPs would file replies within four weeks.
body:
• The Supreme Court termed the three-month delay in deciding disqualification petitions against 20 rebel TMC MPs a "red flag" but set no fixed deadline for Speaker Om Birla.
  • Abhishek Banerjee filed 20 petitions on June 18 alleging the MPs voluntarily gave up TMC membership by joining the NCPI, under the Tenth Schedule.
  • Solicitor General Tushar Mehta opposed a judicial deadline, saying all parties must be heard; the rebel MPs sought four weeks to file replies.
  • The Court kept the petition alive, will monitor progress, and posted the matter after six weeks.

The Supreme Court has termed the three-month delay in deciding disqualification petitions against 20 rebel Trinamool Congress (TMC) MPs a "red flag", while refraining from prescribing a fixed deadline for Lok Sabha Speaker Om Birla to conclude the proceedings. A bench of Chief Justice of India Surya Kant and Justices Joymalya Bagchi and V. Mohana was hearing a plea by TMC MP Abhishek Banerjee seeking expeditious disposal of the petitions, India Legal reported.

Justice Bagchi questioned why the proceedings remained pending after three months, noting that delays in such matters affect collateral proceedings and the democratic process. At the same time, the bench acknowledged that the Speaker is a constitutional authority and that the time needed can vary with the nature and complexity of the dispute.

"There are cases and cases. A few months may be a red flag and that is well taken... three months have lapsed. Why have you not finished it, when it is a matter of moments and has repercussions in various collateral proceedings and also the democratic process of the country?"

Context & Background

The dispute began in June, when 20 TMC Lok Sabha MPs broke away from the party, announced they had joined the Nationalist Citizens Party of India (NCPI), and sought recognition as a separate group in the Lok Sabha. On June 18, Banerjee filed 20 separate disqualification petitions before the Speaker, alleging the MPs had voluntarily given up their TMC membership and were liable to disqualification under the Tenth Schedule of the Constitution, the anti-defection law, according to LawChakra.

https://x.com/RoyR23377/status/2113194339673444779

Senior Advocate Kalyan Banerjee, appearing for Abhishek Banerjee, told the Court that notices were issued to the MPs on August 5, requiring a response within 14 days. After the MPs sought more time, the deadline was extended until September 22, and a further extension was then sought. He argued the proceedings could not remain pending indefinitely. The bench referred to Keisham Meghachandra Singh v. Speaker, Manipur Legislative Assembly, where the Court held that disqualification petitions should ordinarily be decided within a reasonable period, indicating three months as the outer limit in the absence of exceptional circumstances, and that prolonged inaction by a Speaker could be subject to judicial review.

Impact/Analysis

For the Speaker, Solicitor General Tushar Mehta opposed setting a judicial deadline, arguing that the Speaker understands his obligations, that all parties must be given a fair opportunity, and that the proceedings could involve evidence and detailed submissions. The Court's handling reflects that tension: it reminded the Speaker of the responsibility attached to the office without directing him. Justice Bagchi noted the Speaker's distinct constitutional function as head of the legislature and observed, in self-reflection, that the judiciary itself often falls short of its own procedural timelines. CJI Surya Kant said the Court intended to "keep this petition alive" and obtain an update after a reasonable period.

Nothing has been decided on disqualification itself. In Lok Sabha records the 20 MPs remain listed as Trinamool members, the Speaker is yet to rule, and whether their conduct attracts the Tenth Schedule or falls within an exception remains for the Speaker to determine.

What's Next

The case was posted after six weeks. The Solicitor General informed the Court that the MPs were in the process of filing their replies and would require approximately four weeks to do so, and senior advocates for the rebel MPs undertook that replies would be filed within four weeks. The Supreme Court will take an update on the Speaker's proceedings at the next hearing, keeping pressure on the timeline without imposing one.
